div.head: Hu 8
div.ab: Hryðeres belle, hundes hoppe, blæshorn: ðissa ðreora ælc bið anes scill' weorð; ⁊ ælc is melda geteald.
Pecoris tinnitum (tintinnum) et canis hoppa et blophorn (blauhornum): horum trium singulum est unum solidum ualens; et unumquodque reputatum est (reputatur) melda (id est manifestatio).

Nola bouis, collarium canis (Anglice dicitur ‘hundes hoppe’, quasi canis circularium, quia hóp: circulus), tuba cornea: horum trium unumquodque ualet unum sol.; et uniuscuiusque modus computatus [melda].
Hryðeres belle, hundes hoppe, blæshorn—ðissa ðreora ælc bið anes scill' weorð; ⁊ ælc is melda geteald.
Rindes Glocke, Hundes Halsband, Blasehorn: dieser dreier jedes ist 1 Schill. werth; und jedes wird als Anzeiger gerechnet.
An ox's bell, a dog's collar, a blowing-horn: each of these three is worth 1 shilling; and each is reckoned as an informer.
A cow’s bell, a dog’s collar and a horn for blowing—each of these three shall be worth a shilling, and each is reckoned as an informer.
A cow’s bell, a dog’s collar [?], a blast-horn; each of these three is worth a shilling, and each is reckoned an informer.

Cons identifiziert irrig hoppe mit hōp ‘Reifen’ (bei Napier Lexicon 39). Toller nach Thorpe erklärt hoppe ‘Halsglocke (?)’, zitiert aber Ælfreds Übersetzung von anulos bullasque: hring ⁊ hoppan. Den Hund (s. d. Gl 2b) aber behängt man nicht wie Rind, Pferd und Kleinvieh mit einer Glocke, sondern bezeichnet ihn durchs Halsband; Geffcken Lex Sal. 112; Heyne Nahrung 221; Rörig Jagd Fränk. Zeit 21. Das Wort muss selten sein, da Q es unübersetzt lässt und Cons erklärungsbedürftig hält

Cons wrongly identifies hoppe with hōp ‘hoop’ (in Napier Lexicon 39). Toller, following Thorpe, explains hoppe as ‘neck-bell (?)’, but cites Ælfred’s translation of anulos bullasque: hring ⁊ hoppan. The dog (see that word in Gl 2b), however, is not hung with a bell like cattle, horses and small livestock, but is marked by its collar; Geffcken Lex Sal. 112; Heyne Nahrung 221; Rörig Jagd Fränk. Zeit 21. The word must be rare, since Q leaves it untranslated and Cons thinks it needs explaining
Vgl. Gl Horn 2. Toller Suppl. verzeichnet nur hierher blæshorn, ausserdem blæd-, blæsthorn. Zur Form des Q vgl. ebd.: blawan ‘blasen, z. B. ein Horn’
Cf. Gl Horn 2. Toller Suppl. records blæshorn only for this passage, and also blæd-, blæsthorn. For the form in Q cf. ibid.: blawan ‘to blow, e.g. a horn’

Die Sache an und für sich galt weniger; die rechtliche Wichtigkeit, der durch den Verlust mögliche Schaden erklärt die Höherbewertung. Der Glossator der Cons in Cb gibt alternativ, weniger zutreffend, daneben einen anderen Grund: er meint wohl, des Hirten oder des Wanderers Ehre leide, da seine Integrität beim Verluste jener Symbole verdächtig werde

The object in and of itself was worth less; its legal importance, the damage that its loss could cause, explains the higher valuation. The glossator of Cons in Cb gives another reason as an alternative alongside this, less aptly: he probably means that the herdsman’s or the traveller’s honour suffers, since his integrity becomes suspect on the loss of those symbols
Vgl. Gl Anzeiger 2f.
Cf. Gl Anzeiger 2f.

The last two regulations seem utterly foreign to the rest of the ordinance both in style and content. It seems probable, as Liebermann suggests, that they were originally anonymous legal notices, similar to Be Blaserum and Be Forfange, which were appended to the ordinance in the archetype and have been copied in all three MSS as if they formed part of it.

The meaning of the word hoppe is quite uncertain. It is found as the translation of bulla in Alfred’s Orosius, Bk. iv. Chap. x (see BT. p. 552, s.v. hoppe). Liebermann considers it to refer here to the collar which is the distinguishing mark of a dog, but is it not possible that a small disc, presumably inscribed with the owner’s particular mark, may have been attached to the collar and may here be described as hoppe?
No other instance of the form blæshorn is noted by Toller (see Suppl. p. 96). Blædhorn and blæsthorn are found elsewhere.
